title: Criticality-Aware Multi-Criteria Data Routing for Heterogeneous Oil and Gas Telecommunication Links: Design and a Simulation Study of Its Claims
abstract: Remote oil and gas sites reach the control centre over several links with different cost, delay and reliability. We describe a routing system that classifies each data stream as critical or non-critical, scores the available links (Ethernet, 5G, satellite) on latency, loss, bandwidth, cost and reliability with weights from a Fuzzy Analytic Hierarchy Process, moves critical streams after an event-driven fault detection and non-critical streams after a timeout, and damps score-driven switching. The submitted abstract of this work reported a cost reduction of up to 40%, an uptime of 99.97% and a failover below 50 ms, without a reproducible data source. We implemented the system, wrote 24 unit tests, and tested these three claims in an event-based simulation of 100 random 30-day fault scenarios, against a static primary/backup rule, a QoS-only rule and three ablations. All link parameters and fault rates are assumptions and no hardware was used. Under the assumed 3:1 cost ratio between the Ethernet and the 5G link, the proposed rule cut cost by 62.8% against the QoS-only rule; the reduction fell to zero when the 5G link cost two-thirds of the Ethernet link. Critical-stream failover after a link-down event took 35 ms against 1005 ms for the QoS-only rule and 3005 ms for the static rule, but this follows from the assumed 30 ms detection delay. Critical availability exceeded 99.999% for every rule, so the reported 99.97% was not reproduced and the policies are hardly distinguishable on it. Packet loss of the critical stream fell from 5.3e-05 to 8.9e-08. Contrary to the abstract, non-critical traffic switched more often with the proposed rule (4.9 per day) than with the baselines (0.1 to 0.3 per day), because it prefers the less reliable cheap link; damping removed the 2.6 noise-driven switches per day of an undamped rule. The system is at technology readiness level 4; measurements on real links are the next step.

Under the assumed 3:1 cost ratio between the Ethernet and the 5G link, the proposed rule cut cost by 62.8% against the QoS-only rule; the reduction fell to zero when the 5G link cost two-thirds of the Ethernet link. Keywords: data routing; Fuzzy AHP; failover; industrial telecommunication; oil and gas
1. Introduction

Offshore platforms and remote fields depend on telecommunication links of very different kinds: industrial Ethernet or microwave backbones, cellular 5G coverage and satellite. They differ in delay, capacity, loss, price and how often they fail. Control commands and safety alarms need a reliable, low-delay path, whereas video, historian back-fills and software updates need capacity at a low price. A static primary/backup rule treats all traffic alike, sends everything over the best link, and recovers from a fault only when a timer expires.

Multi-criteria decision making is a natural way to choose among links when several criteria conflict (Zionts, 1979). The Analytic Hierarchy Process derives criteria weights from pairwise judgments (Saaty, 1980), and its fuzzy variants let the judgments be imprecise (Buckley, 1985). Fast recovery from link faults depends on link-layer fault signalling, for example bidirectional forwarding detection (Katz and Ward, 2010).

This paper describes a routing system that combines these parts and tests the claims made for it in the abstract submitted to a conference: a cost reduction of up to 40%, an uptime of 99.97% for critical data, a failover below 50 ms, and fewer unnecessary switching events. The abstract did not come with a reproducible data source. We therefore built the system and a simulation, and we report what the simulation supports and what it does not.
2. System design

The system has four parts. A monitor keeps the measured state of each link (delay, loss, bandwidth, cost, reliability). A classifier labels each stream as critical (control commands, safety alarms, shutdown signals, pressure, temperature and flow readings) or non-critical (video, bulk historian data, logs, updates, voice, backups); unknown stream types are treated as critical. A decision module scores each link with a weighted sum of five criteria. An adaptive router moves each stream independently.

Weights. Weights come from a Fuzzy AHP with triangular fuzzy numbers on a linguistic scale (equal, moderate, strong, very strong). We used Buckley's geometric-mean method and a consistency check on the modal values, and rejected judgments with a consistency ratio above 0.1. Two judgment sets were written: for critical traffic reliability dominates, followed by delay and loss, and cost matters little; for non-critical traffic cost dominates, followed by reliability and bandwidth (Table 1). The judgments are our own and would be set with the operator's engineers.
Table 1. Fuzzy AHP weights (consistency ratio 0.060 for the critical and 0.034 for the non-critical profile).

Scoring. Each criterion is mapped to (0, 1] with a saturating function and fixed reference values (50 ms, 0.5% loss, 50 Mbps, a cost of 2). Critical traffic is further restricted to links with delay up to 100 ms, loss up to 1% and bandwidth of at least 1 Mbps; a link that fails these limits is used only when no other link is healthy.

Routing. A critical stream is moved by an event: a link-down signal is assumed to arrive after 30 ms (three 10 ms hello intervals) and the switch takes 5 ms; a degradation is noticed after a 1 s monitoring window. A non-critical stream is moved after a timeout (5 s for a link-down, 30 s for a degradation). After a fault, a stream returns to its preferred link once that link has been fault-free for 30 s (make-before-break, no loss). Score-driven re-selection is damped: another link must beat the current one by a margin of 0.05 on ten consecutive measurements.
3. Simulation study

Links. Three links with assumed parameters: Ethernet or microwave (8 ms, 200 Mbps, cost 3.0 per MB in relative units, availability 0.999), 5G (30 ms, 150 Mbps, cost 1.0, availability 0.98) and satellite (550 ms, 20 Mbps, cost 8.0, availability 0.995). The offered load is 0.1 Mbps of critical and 2 Mbps of non-critical traffic.

Faults. Each link has Poisson link-down episodes and degradation episodes (loss of 2% to 30%) with lognormal durations; the mean time between outages is 20, 2 and 5 days for Ethernet, 5G and satellite. Faults on different links are independent. We generated 100 random 30-day scenarios.

Policies. The proposed system; a static primary/backup rule (Ethernet, then 5G, then satellite, 3 s timeout, degradations never noticed); a QoS-only rule (scores without a cost factor, no classes, 1 s detection); and three ablations of the proposed system that remove the classification, remove the event-driven detection for critical streams (3 s timeout instead), or remove the cost factor for non-critical streams.

Metrics. Availability of the critical stream (one minus the time the path is down or a switch is under way), the fraction of critical packets lost, the failover time after a link-down event, the worst gap, the cost per day, switches per day for each class, and the fraction of time the non-critical stream was unserved (its data are buffered, not lost). The steady-state switching study uses 10 days of measurements at 1 Hz with measurement noise and delay spikes and no faults. Intervals are bootstrap 95% intervals over scenarios.
4. Results

Overall comparison. Table 2 gives the means over 100 scenarios of 30 days. Critical availability was above 99.999% for all rules, so the claim of 99.97% was not reproduced and availability hardly separates the rules. What separates them is the time to recover and the packets lost: after a link-down event the critical stream was moved after 35 ms by the proposed rule, 1005 ms by the QoS-only rule and 3005 ms by the static rule. The 35 ms figure is the assumed detection delay plus switching time, so it shows that the logic adds no delay of its own, not that hardware reaches it. The worst gap of the proposed rule over a scenario, about 1.0 s, comes from degradations, which are noticed after the 1 s monitoring window.
Table 2. Mean results over 100 scenarios of 30 days (assumed link parameters and fault rates; cost in relative units).

Cost. Against the QoS-only rule the proposed system lowered the cost by 62.8% (95% interval 62.8 to 62.8), and by 62.8% against the static rule, because the bulky non-critical traffic moved to the cheaper 5G link. The ablation without classification cost as much as the baselines. This result follows from the assumed prices: when the 5G cost per MB was raised from 1.0 to 2.0 against 3.0 for Ethernet, the reduction fell to zero, because the weighted score then preferred the more reliable Ethernet link (Table 3). The reduction was 78.5% when 5G cost 0.5.
Table 3. Dependence of the cost reduction on the assumed price of the 5G link (20 scenarios per row).

Switching. The claim that criticality-aware differentiation reduces unnecessary switching was not supported on real faults: non-critical traffic switched 4.9 times per day with the proposed rule, against 0.09 (static) and 0.28 (QoS-only), because the proposed rule prefers the cheap 5G link, which fails every two days on average, and returns to it after each fault. In the fault-free noise study, damping removed the switching of an undamped score-driven rule (2.6 switches per day without damping, 0.0 with it, 10 days).

Sensitivity. With four times the fault rate the proposed rule remained the best on critical availability and packet loss (Table 4). Longer event-driven detection delays raised the packet loss but changed the availability little (Table 5).
Table 4. Critical availability when fault rates are multiplied (25 scenarios per row).
Table 5. Effect of the assumed event-driven detection delay on the proposed rule (25 scenarios per row).
5. Discussion and limitations

Of the four claims, one is supported in direction and none in the stated size. A criticality-aware rule does move bulk traffic to the cheaper link and can cut cost, but the size depends on the price ratio of the links; the threshold at which the weighted score stops doing so is a design finding that the original abstract did not give. Faster recovery follows from the assumed fault signalling. The uptime claim was not reproduced because, with independent link faults and three links, every rule had an availability above 99.999%; a figure near 99.97% would need correlated faults (for example a storm affecting 5G and satellite) or a slower recovery than modelled. The claim of fewer unnecessary switches holds only for score-driven noise, where damping helps, and not for the total.

Limits. All parameters are assumed: link properties, prices, fault processes, offered loads, detection delays and the Fuzzy AHP judgments. Faults are independent and links are never congested. The simulation has no packet queue, no protocol behaviour and no security model, and non-critical data are assumed to be buffered without overflow. Failover time is not measured on hardware. The weights depend on judgments that we wrote ourselves.

Next steps. Measure delay, loss, outages and prices on a real platform for at least a month; fit the fault processes including correlated faults; test failover on router hardware with fault signalling; run the controller in shadow mode beside the SCADA network; and set the judgments with the operator's engineers.
6. Conclusion

A criticality-aware, Fuzzy-AHP-based routing rule can keep critical traffic on the most reliable link, recover from link-down events without adding delay of its own, and move bulk traffic to a cheaper link, but its cost benefit depends on the price ratio of the links and it switched non-critical traffic more often than static rules. The 99.97% uptime and the 40% cost reduction of the earlier abstract were not reproduced. The work is at technology readiness level 4 on simulated faults.
Implementation and reproducibility

The study is the repository articles-adaptive-data-routing-og-telecom. Code: src/ogrouting; tests: 24 unit tests (python -m pytest); the study: python research/run_study.py --seeds 100 --days 30, output research/results.json (run on 2026-11-05, Linux, Python 3.13, NumPy).
Data and code availability
All data are produced by the simulator; no field data exist. The code is the author's private repository and is available on request.
